lesson.title: Adding and Subtracting Fractions in Real Life
lesson.description: Learn to add and subtract fractions with different denominators using real-life examples.
lesson.content:
When fractions have different {{term:denominators}}, we cannot add or subtract them directly. We first find the {{term:Lowest Common Denominator}} (LCD) and change each fraction into an {{term:equivalent fraction}} with that denominator. For {{example:1/4 + 1/3}}, the LCD of 4 and 3 is 12, so 1/4 becomes 3/12 and 1/3 becomes 4/12.

Adding the equivalent fractions gives $\frac{3}{12}+\frac{4}{12}=\frac{7}{12}$, so the tailor uses 7/12 of a metre of cloth in total. The same method works for subtraction, as shown next.

For {{example:3/4 - 1/6}}, the LCD of 4 and 6 is 12, so 3/4 becomes 9/12 and 1/6 becomes 2/12. Subtracting gives $\frac{9}{12}-\frac{2}{12}=\frac{7}{12}$, meaning the farmer has 7/12 of a bag of maize left. Now try working out $\frac{2}{5}+\frac{1}{4}$ on your own using the same steps.

questions.question: The picture shows fraction bars for $\frac{1}{4}$ and $\frac{1}{3}$. What is the Lowest Common Denominator (LCD) of 4 and 3?
questions.explanation: LCD is the smallest number both 4 and 3 divide into evenly.
optionExplanations: LCD is the smallest number both 4 and 3 divide into evenly.
questions.feedbackIncorrect: Review this skill and try again.

distractors.misconception: Added the two denominators together
Chose the smaller denominator only
Chose the larger denominator only

reviewRationale: 12 is correct because it is the smallest number that both 4 and 3 divide into exactly, making it the true lowest common denominator.
This comes from wrongly adding 4+3=7, treating denominators like ordinary numbers instead of finding their lowest common multiple.
This happens when a learner simply picks one of the given denominators (3) without checking whether the other fraction fits evenly into it.
This happens when a learner picks the larger denominator (4) assuming it automatically works, without checking that 3 divides into it evenly.

questions.question: A tailor uses $\frac{1}{4}$ metre of cloth for a collar and $\frac{1}{3}$ metre for a pocket. How much cloth is used in total?
optionExplanations: Added numerators and denominators straight across
questions.feedbackIncorrect: Review this skill and try again.

distractors.misconception: Added numerators and denominators straight across
Only converted one fraction correctly
Rounded fractions before adding them

reviewRationale: Correct: converting both fractions to twelfths (3/12 and 4/12) and adding numerators gives 7/12, matching the worked example in the lesson.
This results from wrongly adding numerator to numerator and denominator to denominator (1+1 over 4+3) instead of finding a common denominator first.
This happens if only 1/3 is converted to 4/12 but 1/4 is left unconverted, so the learner mistakenly reports the wrong fraction as the total.
This suggests the learner estimated the sum as roughly a half without doing the actual conversion and addition of the two fractions.
steps: Find LCD of 4 and 3, which is 12.

questions.question: What is $\frac{1}{3}$ written as an equivalent fraction with denominator 12?
questions.explanation: Multiply numerator and denominator by 4 to make twelfths.
optionExplanations: Multiply numerator and denominator by 4 to make twelfths.
Confused this with the equivalent of one quarter
Forgot to multiply the numerator too
questions.feedbackIncorrect: Review this skill and try again.

distractors.misconception: Confused this with the equivalent of one quarter
Forgot to multiply the numerator too
Multiplied numerator by 12 instead

reviewRationale: Correct because multiplying both the numerator and denominator of 1/3 by 4 gives 4/12, an equivalent fraction with the required denominator.
3/12 is actually the equivalent of 1/4, so this shows the learner mixed up which original fraction they were converting.
This happens when only the denominator is multiplied by 4 to reach 12, while the numerator is mistakenly left unchanged at 1.
This occurs when the learner multiplies the numerator by 12 (the target denominator) instead of by the scale factor 4 needed to reach twelfths.

questions.question: Amina spent $\frac{1}{2}$ of her pocket money on lunch and $\frac{1}{5}$ on a pen. What fraction of her money did she spend altogether?
questions.explanation: Change to tenths: $\frac{5}{10}+\frac{2}{10}=\frac{7}{10}$ of her money.
optionExplanations: Change to tenths: $\frac{5}{10}+\frac{2}{10}=\frac{7}{10}$ of her money.
Added numerators and denominators straight across
Only counted the pen amount spent
Used a wrong equivalent for one half
questions.feedbackIncorrect: Review this skill and try again.

distractors.misconception: Added numerators and denominators straight across
Only counted the pen amount spent
Used a wrong equivalent for one half

reviewRationale: Correct: converting 1/2 to 5/10 and 1/5 to 2/10, then adding numerators, gives 7/10 as the total fraction of money spent.
This comes from adding numerators and denominators directly (1+1 over 2+5) rather than converting to a common denominator before adding.
This happens if the learner forgets the lunch amount entirely and only reports the smaller pen fraction as the total spent.
This results from wrongly converting 1/2 to 4/10 instead of 5/10, then adding it to 2/10 to get an incorrect total.

questions.question: The diagram shows a bar for $\frac{3}{4}$ with 1 of the shaded parts crossed out. What fraction remains after subtracting $\frac{1}{4}$?
questions.explanation: 3 shaded parts minus 1 crossed-out part leaves 2 parts, so $\frac{2}{4}$.
optionExplanations: 3 shaded parts minus 1 crossed-out part leaves 2 parts, so $\frac{2}{4}$.
Reported the amount removed, not left
Forgot to subtract anything at all
Added the crossed-out part back on
questions.feedbackIncorrect: Review this skill and try again.

distractors.misconception: Reported the amount removed, not left
Forgot to subtract anything at all
Added the crossed-out part back on

reviewRationale: Correct: the bar starts with 3 of 4 parts shaded; crossing out 1 part leaves 2 parts shaded, so the remaining fraction is 2/4.
This happens when the learner names the fraction that was removed (1/4) rather than working out what fraction is left over.
This shows the learner ignored the subtraction shown by the crossed-out part and simply restated the original fraction shaded.
This suggests the learner mistakenly added the crossed-out part back to the total instead of removing it, giving the whole bar.

questions.question: A farmer has $\frac{3}{4}$ of a bag of maize. He sells $\frac{1}{2}$ of a bag. How much maize is left?
optionExplanations: Reported the amount sold, not left
Stopped after converting, forgot to subtract
Forgot to subtract anything at all
questions.feedbackIncorrect: Review this skill and try again.

distractors.misconception: Reported the amount sold, not left
Stopped after converting, forgot to subtract
Forgot to subtract anything at all

reviewRationale: Correct: converting 1/2 to 2/4 and subtracting from 3/4 gives 1/4 bag remaining, matching the farmer example structure in the lesson.
This happens when the learner names the amount sold (1/2) instead of calculating the amount that is left after selling.
This occurs when the learner correctly converts 1/2 to 2/4 but forgets to actually perform the subtraction step from 3/4.
This shows the learner ignored the sale entirely and simply restated the farmer's starting amount of maize as the final answer.
steps: Find LCD of 4 and 2, which is 4.

questions.question: What is the LCD of 4 and 6, needed to work out $\frac{3}{4}-\frac{1}{6}$?
questions.explanation: 12 is the smallest number that both 4 and 6 divide into.
optionExplanations: 12 is the smallest number that both 4 and 6 divide into.
questions.feedbackIncorrect: Review this skill and try again.

distractors.misconception: Added the two denominators together
Multiplied denominators without simplifying result
Chose the larger denominator only

reviewRationale: 12 is correct as it is the smallest number both 4 and 6 divide into evenly, making it the lowest common denominator for these fractions.
This comes from wrongly adding 4+6=10, treating the denominators as ordinary numbers rather than finding their lowest common multiple.
This happens when 4×6=24 is used as the common denominator, which works but is not the lowest, showing it was not simplified.
This happens when a learner picks the larger denominator (6) assuming it works, without checking that 4 divides into it evenly.

questions.question: Juma planned to study for $\frac{2}{3}$ of an hour but stopped $\frac{1}{4}$ of an hour early. How long did he actually study?
questions.explanation: Convert to twelfths then subtract: $\frac{8}{12}-\frac{3}{12}=\frac{5}{12}$ hour.
optionExplanations: Convert to twelfths then subtract: $\frac{8}{12}-\frac{3}{12}=\frac{5}{12}$ hour.
Used only the converted stopping-early fraction
Added the two fractions instead of subtracting
questions.feedbackIncorrect: Review this skill and try again.

distractors.misconception: Simplified incorrectly after subtracting fractions
Used only the converted stopping-early fraction
Added the two fractions instead of subtracting

reviewRationale: Correct: converting 2/3 to 8/12 and 1/4 to 3/12, then subtracting, gives 5/12 hour as the actual study time.
This may come from an incorrect simplification attempt on 5/12, wrongly reducing it to 1/3 which is not equivalent.
This happens when the learner reports only the converted stopping-early fraction (3/12) instead of subtracting it from the planned time.
This results from adding 8/12 and 3/12 instead of subtracting, because the learner misread which operation the problem requires.

questions.question: A ribbon is split into 6 equal parts. The bar model shows $\frac{2}{6}$ shaded blue and $\frac{3}{6}$ shaded red. What fraction of the ribbon is shaded in total?
questions.explanation: Add same-denominator fractions by adding numerators: $2+3=5$ sixths.
optionExplanations: Add same-denominator fractions by adding numerators: $2+3=5$ sixths.
Subtracted the two amounts instead of adding
Wrongly doubled the denominator when adding
questions.feedbackIncorrect: Review this skill and try again.

distractors.misconception: Subtracted the two amounts instead of adding
Added denominators together as well
Wrongly doubled the denominator when adding

reviewRationale: Correct: since both fractions already share denominator 6, adding numerators 2+3=5 gives 5/6 as the total shaded fraction of the ribbon.
This happens when the learner subtracts the blue part from the red part instead of combining both shaded amounts together.
This comes from wrongly adding the denominators too (6+6=12... actually reported as 6/6), confusing whole-number addition with fraction addition.
This occurs when the learner doubles the denominator to 12 while adding numerators, mistakenly applying a rule from finding equivalent fractions.

questions.question: Work out $\frac{5}{6}-\frac{1}{3}$.
optionExplanations: Forgot to subtract anything at all
questions.feedbackIncorrect: Review this skill and try again.

distractors.misconception: Subtracted numerators without converting first
Forgot to subtract anything at all
Subtracted denominators instead of numerators

reviewRationale: Correct: converting 1/3 to 2/6 so both fractions share a denominator, then subtracting numerators 5-2=3, gives 3/6.
This happens when the learner subtracts 5-1=4 directly without converting 1/3 to sixths first, keeping the original denominator 6.
This shows the learner ignored the subtraction and simply restated the first fraction 5/6 as the final answer.
This results from mistakenly subtracting the denominators (6-3=... reported as 1) instead of subtracting the numerators after conversion.
steps: Find LCD of 6 and 3, which is 6.

questions.question: A painter mixes $\frac{1}{3}$ litre of blue paint with $\frac{1}{6}$ litre of white paint. The bar diagram shows both amounts split into sixths. What is the total volume of paint?
questions.feedbackIncorrect: Review this skill and try again.

distractors.misconception: Added numerators and denominators separately
Treated 1/6 as equal to 1/3
Multiplied fractions instead of adding

reviewRationale: Correct: the LCD of 3 and 6 is 6, so 1/3 becomes 2/6, and 2/6+1/6=3/6, which simplifies to 1/2, the correct total volume.
This comes from adding numerators (1+1=2) and denominators (3+6=9) separately, a common but incorrect shortcut when denominators differ.
This happens if the learner assumes 1/6 is the same size as 1/3 and adds 1/3+1/3, ignoring the actual value of the fraction given.
This results from multiplying the two fractions (1/3 x 1/6=1/18) instead of finding a common denominator and adding them together.

questions.question: A shopkeeper spends $\frac{1}{2}$ of her daily earnings on rent and $\frac{1}{5}$ on transport. What fraction of her earnings does she spend in total?
questions.feedbackIncorrect: Review this skill and try again.

distractors.misconception: Wrongly converted 1/5 to 1/10
Added numerators and denominators separately
Subtracted fractions instead of adding

reviewRationale: Correct: LCD of 2 and 5 is 10; 1/2=5/10 and 1/5=2/10, and adding gives 5/10+2/10=7/10, the total fraction spent.
This occurs if the learner correctly converts 1/2 to 5/10 but wrongly converts 1/5 to 1/10 instead of 2/10, giving 6/10 instead of 7/10.
This comes from adding numerators (1+2=3) and denominators (2+5=7) directly without finding a common denominator first.
This results from subtracting the converted fractions (5/10-2/10=3/10) instead of adding them as the problem requires.
steps: Find LCD of 2 and 5, which is 10.

questions.question: Peter jogs for $\frac{1}{6}$ hour, then walks for $\frac{1}{4}$ hour. What fraction of an hour did he spend on both activities?
optionExplanations: Kept original denominator instead of LCD
Added denominators instead of finding LCD
questions.feedbackIncorrect: Review this skill and try again.

distractors.misconception: Kept original denominator instead of LCD
Converted 1/4 to wrong twelfth value
Added denominators instead of finding LCD

reviewRationale: Correct: LCD of 6 and 4 is 12; 1/6=2/12 and 1/4=3/12, and adding these gives 2/12+3/12=5/12 of an hour.
This happens if the learner keeps denominator 6 for both fractions and adds numerators (1+1=2) to get 2/6, which simplifies to 1/3.
This comes from wrongly converting 1/4 to 5/12 instead of 3/12, then adding 2/12+5/12 to get 7/12 by mistake.
This results from adding the two denominators (6+4=10) to form a new denominator instead of correctly finding the LCD of 12.

questions.question: A jug holds $\frac{5}{6}$ litre of juice. Sena pours out $\frac{1}{2}$ litre. The bar model shows a bar split into sixths with some parts crossed out. How much juice is left?
questions.feedbackIncorrect: Review this skill and try again.

distractors.misconception: Assumed half remains without calculating
Subtracted numerators without converting denominators
Wrongly converted 1/2 to 4/6

reviewRationale: Correct: 1/2 converts to 3/6, and 5/6-3/6=2/6, which simplifies to 1/3 litre remaining, matching the crossed-out bar diagram.
This happens if the learner assumes pouring out half the litre means half the juice remains, without actually converting and subtracting the fractions.
This comes from subtracting numerators directly (5-1=4) over the denominator 6, without first converting 1/2 to sixths, giving 4/6=2/3.
This results from wrongly converting 1/2 to 4/6 instead of 3/6, then subtracting 5/6-4/6 to get 1/6 by mistake.

questions.question: A shopkeeper had $\frac{5}{6}$ kg of rice. He sold $\frac{1}{3}$ kg to a customer. How much rice remains?
optionExplanations: Gave amount sold instead of amount left
questions.feedbackIncorrect: Review this skill and try again.

distractors.misconception: Subtracted numerators but added denominators
Wrongly converted 1/3 to 1/6
Gave amount sold instead of amount left

reviewRationale: Correct: LCD of 6 and 3 is 6; 1/3 becomes 2/6, and 5/6-2/6=3/6, which simplifies to 1/2 kg of rice remaining.
This comes from subtracting numerators (5-1=4) but adding denominators (6+3=9) instead of using the correct common denominator of 6.
This happens if the learner wrongly converts 1/3 to 1/6 instead of 2/6, then subtracts 5/6-1/6 to get 4/6, which simplifies to 2/3.
This results from confusing the amount sold with the amount remaining, simply repeating the 1/3 kg figure from the question as the answer.
steps: Find LCD of 6 and 3, which is 6.

questions.question: A movie is $\frac{5}{6}$ hour long. Kevin has watched $\frac{1}{4}$ hour so far. What fraction of the movie is left to watch?
optionExplanations: Gave amount watched instead of amount left
questions.feedbackIncorrect: Review this skill and try again.

distractors.misconception: Wrongly converted 1/4 to 4/12
Gave amount watched instead of amount left
Forgot to convert 5/6 numerator correctly

reviewRationale: Correct: LCD of 6 and 4 is 12; 5/6=10/12 and 1/4=3/12, and 10/12-3/12=7/12 hour of the movie remaining.
This happens if the learner wrongly converts 1/4 to 4/12 instead of 3/12, then subtracts 10/12-4/12 to get 6/12, which simplifies to 1/2.
This comes from simply restating the fraction of the movie already watched (1/4) instead of calculating the remaining fraction.
This results from forgetting to multiply the numerator of 5/6 by 2 when converting, using 5/12 instead of 10/12, giving 2/12 which simplifies to 1/6.

questions.question: A carpenter joins two planks measuring $\frac{2}{5}$ m and $\frac{1}{10}$ m. What is the total length of the joined planks?
questions.feedbackIncorrect: Review this skill and try again.

distractors.misconception: Added numerators and denominators separately
Wrongly converted 2/5 to 2/10
Ignored the second plank's length

reviewRationale: Correct: LCD of 5 and 10 is 10; 2/5 becomes 4/10, and 4/10+1/10=5/10, which simplifies to 1/2 m total length.
This comes from adding numerators (2+1=3) and denominators (5+10=15) directly, ignoring the rule for combining unlike denominators.
This happens if the learner wrongly converts 2/5 to 2/10 instead of 4/10, then adds 2/10+1/10 to get 3/10 by mistake.
This results from only reporting the length of the larger plank (2/5 m) and forgetting to add the second plank's length at all.

questions.question: Rope A measures $\frac{7}{8}$ m and Rope B measures $\frac{3}{4}$ m. The diagram compares both rope lengths as shaded bars. How much longer is Rope A than Rope B?
optionExplanations: Gave Rope B's length instead of the difference
questions.feedbackIncorrect: Review this skill and try again.

distractors.misconception: Wrongly converted 3/4 to 5/8
Subtracted numerator 3 without converting
Gave Rope B's length instead of the difference

reviewRationale: Correct: 3/4 converts to 6/8, and 7/8-6/8=1/8 m, showing exactly how much longer Rope A is compared to Rope B.
This happens if the learner wrongly converts 3/4 to 5/8 instead of 6/8, then subtracts 7/8-5/8 to get 2/8, which simplifies to 1/4.
This comes from subtracting the unconverted numerator 3 from 7 over denominator 8 (7-3=4/8), instead of first converting 3/4 to eighths.
This results from confusing the question and simply reporting Rope B's own length (3/4 m) instead of finding the difference between the ropes.

questions.question: A trader sold $\frac{1}{3}$ of his stock in the morning and $\frac{2}{9}$ in the afternoon. What fraction of his stock did he sell in total?
optionExplanations: Subtracted the fractions instead of adding
questions.feedbackIncorrect: Review this skill and try again.

distractors.misconception: Added numerators and denominators separately
Subtracted the fractions instead of adding
Wrongly converted 1/3 to 2/9

reviewRationale: Correct: LCD of 3 and 9 is 9; 1/3 becomes 3/9, and 3/9+2/9=5/9, the total fraction of stock sold that day.
This comes from adding numerators (1+2=3) and denominators (3+9=12) directly instead of correctly converting to a common denominator first.
This happens if the learner subtracts the converted fractions (3/9-2/9=1/9) instead of adding them, misreading the problem as a difference.
This results from wrongly converting 1/3 to 2/9 instead of 3/9, then adding 2/9+2/9 to get 4/9 by mistake.

questions.question: A water tank was $\frac{1}{2}$ full. Another $\frac{1}{8}$ of a tank was added. How full is the tank now?
questions.feedbackIncorrect: Review this skill and try again.

distractors.misconception: Added numerators and denominators separately
Wrongly converted 1/2 to 2/8
Wrongly converted 1/2 to 5/8

reviewRationale: Correct: LCD of 2 and 8 is 8; 1/2 becomes 4/8, and 4/8+1/8=5/8, showing how full the tank is now.
This comes from adding numerators (1+1=2) and denominators (2+8=10) directly instead of finding the correct common denominator of 8.
This happens if the learner wrongly converts 1/2 to 2/8 instead of 4/8, then adds 2/8+1/8 to get 3/8 by mistake.
This results from wrongly converting 1/2 to 5/8 instead of 4/8, then adding 5/8+1/8 to get 6/8 by mistake.
steps: Find LCD of 2 and 8, which is 8.

questions.question: John saves $\frac{1}{5}$ of his allowance on Monday and $\frac{1}{4}$ on Tuesday. Did he save more than half his allowance over the two days?
options: Yes, he saved more than half
No, he saved less than half
optionExplanations: Assumed adding two fractions always exceeds half
Mistook a close value for exactly half
Thinks fractions with money can't be compared
questions.feedbackIncorrect: Review this skill and try again.

distractors.misconception: Assumed adding two fractions always exceeds half
Mistook a close value for exactly half
Thinks fractions with money can't be compared

reviewRationale: Incorrect: learner likely assumed combining two savings amounts must exceed half without converting to a common denominator to check the actual sum.
Correct: converting to twentieths gives $\frac{4}{20}+\frac{5}{20}=\frac{9}{20}$, which is one twentieth short of the half-mark $\frac{10}{20}$.
Incorrect: learner rounded $\frac{9}{20}$ to 'about half' instead of checking it is strictly less than $\frac{10}{20}$.
Incorrect: the fractions can be compared once expressed with a common denominator; this option reflects avoidance of the calculation.

questions.question: A cook has $\frac{5}{8}$ hour to prepare a meal. She has already used $\frac{1}{4}$ hour. Does she have enough time left to do a task needing $\frac{1}{3}$ hour?
options: Yes, $\frac{3}{8}$ hour is more than $\frac{1}{3}$ hour
No, $\frac{3}{8}$ hour is less than $\frac{1}{3}$ hour
questions.explanation: Remaining time $\frac{3}{8}$ hour is greater than the $\frac{1}{3}$ hour needed.
optionExplanations: Remaining time $\frac{3}{8}$ hour is greater than the $\frac{1}{3}$ hour needed.
Compared fractions by looking at denominators only
Guessed the values matched without converting
questions.feedbackIncorrect: Review this skill and try again.

distractors.misconception: Compared fractions by looking at denominators only
Guessed the values matched without converting

contentBlocks.text: When fractions have different {{term:denominators}}, we cannot add or subtract them directly. We first find the {{term:Lowest Common Denominator}} (LCD) and change each fraction into an {{term:equivalent fraction}} with that denominator. For {{example:1/4 + 1/3}}, the LCD of 4 and 3 is 12, so 1/4 becomes 3/12 and 1/3 becomes 4/12.
Adding the equivalent fractions gives $\frac{3}{12}+\frac{4}{12}=\frac{7}{12}$, so the tailor uses 7/12 of a metre of cloth in total. The same method works for subtraction, as shown next.

For {{example:3/4 - 1/6}}, the LCD of 4 and 6 is 12, so 3/4 becomes 9/12 and 1/6 becomes 2/12. Subtracting gives $\frac{9}{12}-\frac{2}{12}=\frac{7}{12}$, meaning the farmer has 7/12 of a bag of maize left. Now try working out $\frac{2}{5}+\frac{1}{4}$ on your own using the same steps.
